tools.name: bb_search
tools.description: Unified indexed retrieval for symbol lists, content, exact symbol source, or files. This is retrieval, not natural-language explanation or code analysis. Symbol/content/file modes carry a freshness block ({ fresh, stale, missing, staleRatio, mode, remediation }) stating whether results reflect the current files; rows may carry stale=true. Remediation names the exact reindex command. When a read finds stale/missing files within budget, the handler auto-refreshes exactly those files (reindexFilesParallel) before answering and declares it in an autoRefresh field; refresh=false opts out and answers from existing data with the staleness block. Every response declares its match set: totalMatches is the number of matching symbols the page was cut from (not the page size) and truncated is true when a candidate cap or the noise filter kept matches out, so a short page is never mistaken for a complete one. Options a mode cannot honor are rejected with an error naming that mode's accepted options, never silently ignored. Content mode also declares HOW it matched: matchMode is phrase when the query appeared verbatim in the name, qualified name, docstring or symbol body, and terms when nothing matched verbatim and the query's content words were matched instead — a phrase hit means the code contains this text, a terms hit means it discusses the same words, which is weaker evidence. It declares bodyCoverage ({ withBody, symbols, ratio }) because a project indexed before bodies were stored has no searchable body at all, so 'nothing matched' from such a project means something different from 'nothing could match'. language and symbolKind are matched case-insensitively against the indexed vocabulary, and a value the index does not contain is reported as an error rather than as zero results.

query.description: symbol/content/regex query, trimmed before use; also accepted as the exact symbol name in symbol mode. Not accepted in file mode

symbolName.description: exact symbol name for symbol mode; supplying it with a different query is an error

filePath.description: file target for file mode, or symbol disambiguation in symbol mode. Not accepted in symbols/content modes

limit.description: max results (default 15); 0 returns no rows; must be a whole number. symbols/content/symbol modes only

language.description: filter by language, case-insensitive (e.g. typescript, python, go); a language this project does not index is an error. symbols/content modes only

symbolKind.description: filter by symbol kind, case-insensitive (function, class, variable, interface, enum, ...); a kind this project does not index is an error. symbols/content modes only

includeContent.description: include a code snippet per result (default false). symbols mode only

exact.description: only exact name matches (default false); obeys caseSensitive. symbols mode only

caseSensitive.description: case-sensitive matching (default false); folds every Unicode case pair, not only ASCII. symbols mode only

regex.description: treat query as a regex against symbol names (default false). symbols mode only

refresh.description: false opts out of the inline auto-refresh of stale files (default: auto-refresh within budget before answering)

documentation.summary: Unified lexical, content, exact-symbol, and file retrieval.

returns: Indexed matches with file and line provenance
Exact symbol or bounded file source in retrieval modes
Freshness state where available
errors: Missing mode-specific query, symbolName, or filePath
limitations: Results reflect the current index and may be stale
Content search is lexical; use bb_ask for semantic discovery
tools.performance: Pagination and result limits bound retrieval; exact indexed lookup is preferred over content scanning.
tools.safety: Read-only. It does not refresh the index or modify source files.
tools.evidence: Paths, line ranges, symbol kinds, and source snippets are indexed evidence; stale flags qualify that evidence.

tools.name: bb_ask
tools.description: Answer a question about the codebase using semantic search over the index. Returns matched symbols with similarity scores.
returns: Natural-language answer
Ranked semantic matches
Similarity and source provenance
limitations: Semantic similarity discovers candidates but does not independently prove a claim
Local word vectors provide lexical-quality fallback rather than model-quality semantics
tools.performance: The limit bounds returned semantic matches; embedding coverage and model choice affect ranking quality.
tools.safety: Read-only. It does not write source or silently rebuild embeddings.
tools.evidence: Treat matched symbols and resolvable source locations as evidence; treat generated explanation as interpretation.

tools.name: bb_health
tools.description: Unified index health: file/symbol/relationship/imports counts, embedding model + coverage, schema version, runtime, and file freshness. Use verbose=true for per-language breakdown and stale-file names, refresh=true to reindex before reporting, force=true to force a full in-place reindex before reporting, integrity=true for the 12-point index health check, complete=true for full (not sampled) freshness, includeAnalysisRuns=true for persisted run/finding totals, history=true for persisted analysis history.

force.description: force a full in-place reindex before reporting

wait.description: wait for refresh to finish (default true)

documentation.summary: Unified index, schema, freshness, embeddings, runtime, integrity, and analysis history.

returns: Index, schema, runtime, freshness, and embedding health
Optional integrity and analysis-history summaries
Typed warnings and refresh outcome
limitations: Sampled freshness is not a complete filesystem proof
Embedding coverage reports stored state, not semantic quality
tools.performance: Sampled freshness is the default; complete freshness and integrity checks intentionally cost more.
tools.safety: Status is read-only. refresh=true explicitly mutates only index data; force=true performs a full in-place reindex.
tools.evidence: Counts and versions come from the brain database; freshness compares indexed metadata with the filesystem.

tools.name: bb_patterns
tools.description: Detect orphaned code, framework patterns, and anti-patterns, ranked by evidence-derived confidence, with staleness markers when a finding's file changed after indexing. Use scope=orphaned for dead code; scope=all (default) for the full pattern scan with the optional pattern/confidence filters. Architecture and code-quality analysis are planned, not yet executable.

scope.description: orphaned only, or all pattern classes (default all)

includeOrphaned.description: include orphaned-code patterns in an all scan (default true)

confidenceThreshold.description: drop findings below this confidence (default 0 = report everything, ranked). Orphan confidence is evidence-derived and spans 0.3-0.7; anti-pattern confidence is 0.6-0.9

recordRun.description: persist this scan as an analysis run (persists the whole census, not the displayed page)

documentation.summary: Pattern/orphan analysis ranked by evidence-derived confidence, with optional persisted run history.

returns: Pattern findings with confidence and locations
Orphan, framework, and anti-pattern classifications
Optional persisted run history
limitations: A finding is not a deletion instruction. The tool reports what the index does and does not record; where the index is silent, the finding says so on its face rather than presenting absence of evidence as evidence of absence.

Confidence is derived from measured evidence classes, not assigned per rule. It spans 0.30-0.70 for orphans (the published cap) and 0.60-0.90 for anti-patterns. Name-unique symbols measured a 0.0% false-positive rate against a source-text oracle; ambiguous names measured 14.4%.

A symbol with no ANCHORED incoming row, in a file that has one, gets the coverage-gap disclosure. The per-symbol test counts anchored rows only while the per-file test counts any row, and that asymmetry is deliberate: an unanchored row is a name match, and 97% of rake's `references` edges name no consumer, so counting them per symbol would suppress the disclosure across the whole corpus.

A framework-detected finding carries a FIXED confidence of 0.6, not one derived from how much evidence supports it, and there is a consequence worth knowing before you use confidenceThreshold: asking for more than 0.6 removes every framework finding at once. Measured on ten repositories, framework findings are constant at thresholds 0, 0.5 and 0.6, and zero at 0.61, 0.7 and 0.9 — including on a project where the indexer had assigned 40 distinct framework types. The answer is not wrong, since the finding's confidence genuinely is 0.6, but a threshold intended to exclude weak findings cannot discriminate among these at all.

A relationship only counts as usage evidence if it is not a self-loop, its published evidenceClass is not "inferred", and its confidence is at least 0.7. Refused rows are counted in `summary.unverifiedUsageEdges` and itemised on the findings they would have cleared.

A finding whose symbol had no recorded incoming reference while its file did carries a COVERAGE GAP INDICATOR. That is the signature of an analyzer that reached the file and not the symbol, and such a finding may be a coverage gap rather than dead code.
Dynamic dispatch, reflection, and string-keyed lookups are invisible. The engine never fabricates a resolved edge for them, so a symbol reached only that way is reported.
False-positive rate is 0.0-27.8% by corpus, measured against a source-text oracle that cannot see reflection or template indirection — so the true rate is higher, and the number is a lower bound.

Test files are excluded from candidates but not from evidence: a production symbol called only from a test is not reported, and a production file imported only by a test is not reported. `includeTests: true` means "also report test symbols", not "ignore tests when looking for users".
Framework and anti-pattern detection is heuristic and confidence-qualified.
tools.performance: Cost is index-bound and grows with the SYMBOL count, not the relationship count: every set the scan builds is reduced in SQL, so a 223,880-symbol / 898,806-relationship repository is scanned in 32s and a 56,738-symbol one in 3.9s. Three measurements on real corpora, each with byte-identical output: the anti-pattern rules once took 330s because of a correlated COUNT and now take 0.4s; the relationship pass once shipped 710,671 rows into JS to build sets bounded by symbol count and now ships ~5,700 rows of aggregates; and the whole scan was three statements over the same rows before the coverage indicator re-read what the evidence gate had already read. `limit` bounds the displayed page; the census in the header is the full candidate count, and `raise \`limit\`` is named when the page is short.
tools.safety: Source is read-only. recordRun writes only analysis-history records in the brain database, and persists the whole census rather than the displayed page so the auto-resolve pass cannot mark live findings as gone.
tools.evidence: Every finding is confidence-qualified, carries an evidence array naming what was checked, and carries a limitations array. Two channels are kept distinct: an anchored edge from an identified symbol is decisive, while a name match clears a candidate only when the name is unambiguous in the reporting scope. `summary.suppressedByReason` accounts for every candidate the scan discarded, and `summary.importResolution` states how far the import channel could be carried.

tools.name: bb_security
tools.description: Taint-flow security scan over the indexed source-to-sink flows: SQL injection, XSS, command injection, path traversal, insecure deserialization, SSRF, open redirect and code execution. Flows whose endpoints both resolve to indexed symbols are findings; one-sided flows are reported separately as unvalidated observations, never as confirmed exploits. Findings whose underlying file changed after indexing carry a staleness marker.

recordRun.description: persist this scan as an analysis run

documentation.summary: Taint-flow findings over the index, with optional persisted run history. A flow is a finding only when both endpoints resolve to indexed symbols; one-sided flows are reported as unvalidated observations. Every response states the census so a capped scan is never mistaken for a complete one. Not detected: hardcoded secrets; genuine cross-language taint; standalone weak crypto.

returns: Normalized security findings (label, severity, calibrated confidence, sink type, source type)
A `[scan: …]` census line stating how many taint flows were indexed, how many findings they deduplicated into, how many are being shown, and how many are beyond the cap
One-sided flows listed separately as unvalidated observations, each with its real severity and the reason it is unvalidated
Optional persisted run history, recording the full analysed finding set (never the display window) with evidence, confidence and limitations
errors: Unknown option (rejected with the accepted set named)
limitations: Static taint analysis can produce false positives and false negatives
It is not runtime testing or a penetration test

`confirmed` means both flow endpoints are indexed symbols — it does **not** prove the values are connected. The indexer pairs every taint source with every taint sink in a symbol body, so two tokens in one function produce a confirmed flow whether or not one reaches the other

**Not detected:** hardcoded secrets (no such finding type is emitted; that rule belongs to `bb_patterns`), genuine cross-*language* taint (the `crossLanguage` flag means the flow was stitched across symbols, not that languages differ), standalone weak-crypto use (emitted as a sink with no co-located source, so it remains an observation)
Severity is normalized into exactly `critical|high|medium|low|unknown`; an unrecognised stored value becomes `unknown` rather than vanishing from the counts
tools.performance: Indexed flow analysis and output/history limits bound work and response size. The response always states the census — indexed flows, deduplicated findings, findings shown, findings beyond the cap — so a truncated scan is never presented as a complete one. `recordRun` re-scans with a census-sized cap so that persisting the history snapshot can never auto-resolve findings that were merely not examined.
tools.safety: Source is read-only. recordRun writes only analysis-history records in the brain database.
tools.evidence: A finding is supported by indexed source/sink locations and relationship paths; severity does not imply exploitability. Persisted history records the engine's calibrated confidence (0.7 confirmed / 0.4 observation / 0.3 mitigated), the taint-flow evidence, and the per-finding limitations. Unvalidated observations are never persisted to history.

tools.name: bb_visualize
tools.description: Scoped dependency and architecture visualization over the canonical graph engine, with explicit filters, provenance, truncation, machine-readable JSON, and genuinely self-contained HTML (no network, no fonts, no build step — it renders offline, in an air-gapped editor, anywhere). The answer is an AUDITABLE projection of the index, not a picture: every link carries the stored relationship row it traces to (rowId) and its stored confidence, and every node carries its line, lineEnd and qualifiedName, so the graph is navigable and every edge can be checked against the row that justifies it. Distinct relationship types between the same pair are SEPARATE links, so a pair that is both contains and exports renders as both. Node size follows the index’s own gravity score. In the HTML, edge opacity encodes stored confidence, relationship type sets colour and a structural/behavioural dash, and a stale endpoint (file changed since index) is drawn as a hollow ring; links inherit worst-of-endpoints. Every answer declares its bounds as three DISTINCT numbers — totalNodesAvailable (what the scope and filters actually match), truncation.originalNodes (what reached the projection) and nodes (what was returned) — so a short page can never be mistaken for a whole set. Whatever the noise filter removes is counted onto excluded with the patterns responsible, and an empty answer is declaredAbsent with a reason rather than an empty result that looks like a real project. Same owner-cascade semantics as bb_graph: member-level relationships are attributed to the owner class.

target.description: file, module, symbol, or feature target (`symbol`/`symbolName`/`query` are accepted as aliases)

excludePatterns.description: path SEGMENTS treated as build noise and excluded. Matched on whole segments, never as substrings — a substring rule removed `src/util/edit_distance.rs` because `dist` is inside `edit_distance`, and `src/compiler/layout.rs` because `out` is inside `layout`. Omit to use the defaults (node_modules, .git, .next, .turbo, .cache, coverage, dist, build, out, target, vendor, __pycache__)

includeTests.description: include test/spec sources. Default true: they are ordinary source. When false, test/spec/testdata directories and *_test.* / *spec.* files are excluded and counted

documentation.summary: Scoped canonical dependency graphs with explicit truncation and provenance.

returns: Canonical nodes and links, with EVERY stored relationship type between a pair kept as a separate link

An auditable projection rather than a picture: each link carries `rowId` (the stored relationship it traces to), its stored `confidence` and its line; each node carries `line`, `lineEnd` and `qualifiedName`, so the graph is navigable and every edge can be checked against the row that justifies it

Three DISTINCT declared counts — `totalNodesAvailable` (what the scope and filters match), `truncation.originalNodes` (what reached the projection) and `nodes` (what was returned) — so a short page is never mistaken for a whole set
`excluded` — what the noise filter removed, how many, and the patterns responsible — so a partial map is never mistaken for a complete one
`declaredAbsent` with an `absenceNote` when the answer is empty, distinguishing what matched nothing from what matched but did not survive the projection

Text, JSON, or genuinely SELF-CONTAINED HTML: one file with no network, no fonts and no build step, carrying its own force-directed layout and canvas renderer, so it renders offline and in an air-gapped editor

In the HTML the evidence is ENCODED rather than decorated: edge opacity is stored confidence, relationship type sets colour and a structural/behavioural dash, a stale endpoint is a hollow ring, node size is the index's own gravity, and any node or edge can be selected to read its stored facts
errors: Missing target for a scoped graph
limitations: The graph reflects static indexed relationships

NOISE FILTER (declared, and the caller's to change). Build output and VCS metadata are excluded by default, matched on whole path SEGMENTS. This was previously a bare-substring rule that removed real source: measured on cargo, `dist` removed `src/util/edit_distance.rs`, `out` removed `src/compiler/layout.rs` and `src/compiler/output_depinfo.rs`, and `build` removed `crates/cargo-test-support/build.rs`, leaving 225 of 1,787 symbol-bearing files with no exclusion declared anywhere. Test and spec sources are ordinary source and are INCLUDED by default; `excludePatterns` and `includeTests` change all of it, and whatever is removed is counted onto `excluded`

SCOPE TARGETS ARE VALUES, not patterns. `%` and `_` match themselves and a directory prefix matches on a segment boundary, so `src/util` never reaches `src/utilities`. This matches bb_analyze, whose contract states the same rule; the two tools previously disagreed, and this one was the permissive one (measured: a target of `%` selected every file in the corpus)

`feature` scope matches a symbol NAME or a docstring. The docstring half is thin in practice and the answer does not pretend otherwise: measured on cargo, 70 of 40,595 symbols (0.17%) carry one, so a feature query is usually a name match
Nodes and links beyond configured budgets are omitted and reported
Owner-cascade attribution: member-level relationships are attributed to the owner class, same as bb_graph
tools.performance: maxNodes, maxLinks, scope, relationshipTypes, and languages constrain graph construction.
tools.safety: Read-only. HTML output contains the same bounded graph as JSON and does not mutate the project.
tools.evidence: Nodes and links resolve to canonical indexed entities; links with omitted endpoints are not emitted.

tools.name: bb_migrate
tools.description: Read-only single or batch migration planning with dependency order, explicit effort methodology, library mappings, risks, truncation, and unsupported cases. Plans whose source file changed since the last index are flagged stale up front — a plan is a claim about current code; JSON output carries the freshness block.

symbolNames.description: one or more symbols to migrate

documentation.summary: Batch cross-language migration plans with ordering, methodology, and unsupported mappings.

returns: Dependency-ordered migration plans
Effort methodology, library mappings, and risks
Explicit unsupported and truncation results
limitations: Plans are estimates, not translated source
Library mappings are advisory and unsupported routes remain explicit

Dependency ordering and mapping depend on the analyzer-extracted symbol and relationship graph; edge cases that the analyzers cannot resolve (reflection, dynamic dispatch, or cross-file relations the grammar does not model) limit the completeness of the resulting plan
tools.performance: Requests are capped at 100 symbols and dependency traversal is bounded.
tools.safety: Read-only. It does not generate, replace, or compile target-language source.
tools.evidence: Dependency ordering comes from indexed relationships; effort and mappings are labeled methodology-driven estimates.

tools.name: bb_analyze
tools.description: Unified evidence-backed analysis over graph relationships, dependencies, project statistics, complexity, impact, and test intelligence. Select exactly one mode. Every read mode carries a freshness block (fresh/stale/missing counts + remediation) resolved against the live working tree, and report rows carry a stale flag when their file changed after indexing. Every mode is BOUNDED and says so: `limit` is the most items returned (edges per direction for callers/callees/trace, files for dependencies, entries for the test modes, the same everywhere) and the answer reports what it returned against what exists, so a page is never read as the whole set. callers/callees/trace/impact share the graph engine's owner-cascade semantics — a relationship stored against a class member is attributed to the owner class — and every edge states which it was through `targetMatch`. WHICH symbol the name resolved to is declared as well: `rootMatch` is `exact`, `exact-any-kind` or `containment`, and `containment` means the answer is about a symbol whose name CONTAINS the one asked for, or differs only in case — `found: true` on its own does not mean the name was itself a symbol. Locations are project-relative. Per-mode parameters: target applies to callers, callees, trace, complexity, impact, and test_impact; filePath scopes dependencies, test_mapping, test_gaps, and test_quality to a project-relative path PREFIX and is REFUSED (not ignored) on every other mode; limit applies to callers, callees, trace, dependencies, test_mapping, test_gaps and test_quality and is refused elsewhere; stats is always project-wide.

target.description: A symbol name for callers/callees/trace/impact/test_impact, or a project-relative FILE PATH for complexity (an exact file, or a directory prefix at any depth INCLUDING a top-level one; anything else is refused rather than treated as a path fragment). `symbol`/`symbolName`/`query` are accepted as aliases. A target is a VALUE, never a pattern: `%`, `_` and `\` are escaped and match themselves. Echoed back bounded at 200 characters with its full length stated — the search always uses the whole string.

filePath.description: Project-relative path PREFIX scoping dependencies, test_mapping, test_gaps and test_quality. Refused on every other mode. Matched on a whole segment boundary, so `src/util` does not match `src/utilities`.

limit.description: Maximum items returned: edges per direction for callers/callees/trace, files for dependencies, entries for test_mapping/test_gaps/test_quality. Defaults: 25 edges per direction, 20 files, 50 entries. Range 1-5000 (graph modes) or 1-2000 (the rest); 0 and anything above the ceiling are REFUSED rather than clamped, because a returned page must mean the page that was asked for. The answer reports what it returned and whether that is the whole set. Refused on the modes it does not apply to.

documentation.summary: One typed analysis surface over the graph, the file graph, project counts, complexity, impact and test evidence. Every mode is bounded, declares its own bounds, and reports what it returned against what exists.

returns: Mode-specific typed analysis: graph edges, file dependency edges, project counts, complexity metrics, impact, or test evidence
A declared bound on every answer — what was returned, what exists, and whether the set is the whole one
Explicit unavailable states: a metric or target that cannot be computed is `available: false` / `notFoundReason`, never a substituted number
errors: Missing or blank target for a target-based mode
Option irrelevant to the selected mode (refused, never ignored)
`limit` on a mode it does not apply to, or `limit: 0`
A `complexity` target that names no indexed file and no directory prefix
limitations: Static relationships cannot establish runtime behavior
Test results describe indexed static evidence, not executed coverage; a project whose tests the indexer did not recognise is reported as having none, with the reason

Callers/callees/trace/impact modes share the graph engine's owner-cascade semantics: a relationship stored against a class member is attributed to the owner class. Every edge states which it was through `targetMatch` (`exact` or `owner-cascade`); absent means the engine could not tell, which is not the same as `exact`

A name resolves to ONE stored symbol, and WHICH one is declared in `rootMatch`: `exact` (a structural symbol of that name), `exact-any-kind` (a symbol of that name the graph cannot traverse — a constant, a type alias — which still has callers), or `containment`. `containment` is the documented near-miss fallback and means the answer is about a symbol whose name CONTAINS the one asked for. Measured on this repository's src: `target: "us"` answered `found: true` rooted at `analyzeCSharpBareIdentifierUses`, and `target: "_"` answered `found: true` rooted at `build_registry` when no symbol is named `_`. `found: true` alone does not mean the name was a symbol

A CASE difference resolves by containment, because the exact step is `name = ?` (case-sensitive) and SQLite's `LIKE` is case-insensitive for ASCII. So `target: "HUB"` and `target: "hub"` are the same answer, reached by the weaker step — which is why `rootMatch` says `containment` for the first

`limit` has two ends and both are declared: refused below 1 (an empty page is indistinguishable from a real answer) and refused above 5,000 for the graph modes / 2,000 for the rest. It is refused rather than clamped, because a returned page must mean the page that was asked for. Measured on this repository's src, `limit: 2147483648` was accepted before this and answered with the whole corpus

`complexity` accepts a directory prefix at ANY depth, including a top-level directory. It did not: the prefix branch required a `/` in the target, so `target: "ast"` was refused as "no indexed file matches" while 84 indexed files sat under it, and the same for every top-level directory on every project

`complexity` publishes both file counts: `filesMatchingScope` is how many files the scope names and `filesInScope` is how many hold a symbol the metrics are over. They differ when a file in scope has no indexed symbol (83 of 84, measured), and `linesOfCode` covers the second number — so the gap is visible instead of an unexplained discrepancy

`test_mapping.summary.productionSymbols` and `test_gaps.summary.productionSymbols` are the SAME number, and each report also states `excludedAsNoise`, so `productionSymbols + excludedAsNoise` is the store's population under the mode's own filter. `test_gaps.summary.total` is a count of GAPS, not of production symbols — it is the population minus `directlyTested`, and the identity closes in public

A `not-found` answer is bounded: the target is echoed at most 200 characters with its full length stated. A 4,000-character target produced a 9,409-byte answer (~2.6k tokens for two words of information) before this. The bound is on the ECHO only — the search always uses the whole string
A name resolves among several stored symbols. `rootCandidates` says how many — 1 means the name was unique, more means the answer is about one of several

mode `impact` refuses a target the graph cannot root at, with `notFoundReason: "not-traversable"` and the symbol type. Such a symbol IS in the index; `callers`/`callees` resolve the same name because they match any type
A depth-capped walk is TRUNCATION and says so: `summary.truncated` is true with `truncationReason` naming the depth cap, beside `maxDepth` and `maxDepthReached`

A walk also runs under a wall-clock budget (`summary.timeBudgetMs` / `timeBudgetExhausted`, default 2,000 ms). A node is not a unit of work: the per-node caller query is priced by the reproducible ORDER BY, which SQLite applies before the LIMIT, so `edgeLimit` cannot bound it. Measured on this repository's own src: 2,436 matching rows for one symbol cost 85.8 ms of the 87.8 ms, and the walk was unbounded until this budget existed

`dependencies` resolves an internal specifier against the importing file's own directory and LABELS each edge `resolved` / `suffix-match` / `unresolved`. It is not a guess from a basename: on this repository's own src only 74 of 906 `imports` relationships carry both endpoints and `brain_import.resolved_symbol_id` is empty, so specifier resolution is the primary path, not a fallback
A file's `dependents` and `dependencies` lists are capped per row; `dependentsTotal` / `dependenciesTotal` are the real sizes and the Truncated flags say the list was cut

Neither list carries `fileId` — a file id is `<40-hex project id>:<relative path>`, so it repeated the path printed beside it (56,540 of 121,340 bytes on a default page of this repository's src). The path is the locator, `resolution` says how it was reached, and the row above carries the id for the file the row is about

`metrics.couplingEdges` counts only the relationship types listed in `couplingRelationshipTypes`; `exports` and `contains` are index bookkeeping. `stats.relationships` is every row and is a different number
`metrics.maintainability` is unavailable when the formula's domain does not cover the scope (it is negative above roughly 3·10⁴ non-blank lines) rather than clamped to 0
Locations are project-relative. `nodes[].filePath` (absolute) is not emitted, so the same question returns the same bytes on any machine
A mapping entry carries at most 20 links (`linksTruncated` says when more exist); the ranking and every summary count use the complete set
`provenance` on a `dependencies` page is on the REPORT, not repeated per row
tools.performance: Every mode is paged and says so. `limit` bounds the answer — 25 edges per direction for callers/callees/trace (default), 20 files for dependencies, 50 entries for the test modes. On this repository's src (183 files, 8,565 symbols, 52,597 relationships) a default answer is 1.5-26 KB for eight of the eleven modes; `dependencies` is 75.9 KB (~21k tokens) because 20 of those files really do have 506 internal edges between them, so a caller who wants less should pass `limit`. The graph walk is additionally bounded by depth, per-node site limit, fan-out budget, and a wall-clock budget; whichever fires is named in `truncationReason`. All nine graph cases in fixtures/analyze/latency-gate.sh answer in under 2.4 s on that corpus, against a measured 613 s and several that never returned.
tools.safety: Read-only. Analysis never creates tests or edits source.
tools.evidence: Findings derive from brain_* symbols, files, relationships, complexity, and test-file classifications. `provenance.evidenceClass` classifies what kind of claim the answer is; `unknowns` names every absence the answer rests on.

tools.name: bb_doc
tools.description: Generate read-only, evidence-backed documentation with resolvable citations and a freshness block over the cited files. Every mode emits its declared section set, an empty result is never reported as passing, and the token budget is enforced against the whole payload. Supports symbol, file, module, feature, API, project, and documentation-coverage modes in Markdown or JSON. When the cited files are stale, the handler auto-refreshes exactly those files within budget and regenerates the document; refresh=false opts out and answers from existing data with the freshness block.

target.description: symbol, file, module, feature, or API target (`symbol`/`symbolName`/`query` are accepted as aliases); optional for project and coverage

refresh.description: false opts out of the inline auto-refresh of the files this document cites (default: auto-refresh those files within budget, then regenerate)

documentation.summary: Cited Markdown or JSON documentation over indexed source and relationships.

returns: Markdown or structured JSON documentation
Resolvable citations and evidence classifications
Quality and website reference metadata
limitations: Unknown facts remain explicit rather than inferred without support
Stale evidence is qualified and cannot silently become current
tools.performance: Evidence count and maxTokens impose explicit response budgets.
tools.safety: Read-only. It never refreshes implicitly, writes source, or invokes bb_edit.
tools.evidence: Claims are classified as extracted, inferred, generated, or unknown and carry resolvable citations where applicable.

tools.name: bb_edit
tools.description: Unified, validated source mutation. Discriminated by mode: write, update, insert, delete, or refactor. Supports dry-run previews, separator/symlink-safe paths, AST byte bounds, caller protection, rollback on validation failure, formatting, and reindexing. If the target file changed since it was indexed, this tool refreshes that one file and re-resolves the symbol before editing (reported in warnings) — an edit is never applied to stale byte bounds, and a symbol that was renamed or removed is refused by name.

mode.description: Edit kind: write (create or overwrite a file), update (replace a symbol body), insert (add code relative to a symbol), delete (remove a symbol), or refactor (identifier-aware rename)

dryRun.description: Preview the planned changes without writing any file (default false)

filePath.description: write: project-relative target file to create or overwrite. Other modes: disambiguates symbolName when it appears in multiple files

symbolName.description: Name of the symbol to update, delete, or refactor (the index must contain it; a target file changed since indexing is refreshed automatically before the edit)

lineStart.description: Declaration line of the target symbol, used with symbolName/filePath to disambiguate repeated names

content.description: Full file content for write mode; also accepted in place of newContent for update and insert

newContent.description: Replacement source: update swaps the symbol body for this text; insert adds this text relative to targetSymbolName

targetSymbolName.description: insert: symbol whose body or boundary receives the new code (required for insert)

position.description: insert anchor relative to targetSymbolName (default after)

newName.description: refactor: the valid identifier the symbol is renamed to

force.description: delete: allow removal when indexed callers or live references survive; leftovers are reported as warnings (default false)

format.description: Run the project formatter on written files after the edit (default true)

documentation.summary: Unified safe source editing with preview, validation, rollback, and reindex.

returns: Structured mutation result or dry-run preview
Validation, formatting, rollback, and reindex status
Affected paths and caller protection outcomes
errors: Ambiguous symbol name (the message names filePath/lineStart)
Symbol renamed or removed since the target file was indexed (refreshed first, then refused by name)
Caller protection, parse, formatting, or reindex failure
limitations: Named symbol edits need an INDEX, not a fresh one: when the target file changed after it was indexed, the tool refreshes that ONE file's rows and re-resolves the symbol before planning, so bounds always come from the bytes on disk and never from a stale span (M59.A11, #890). The refresh is reported in `warnings`; if the symbol was renamed or removed in the meantime the edit is refused by name instead of guessing a span

Directly after a write, the file's own evidence is current but cross-file relationships are only re-derived within the bounded post-pass, so a caller in an unrelated file may lag until the next dir index (same bound as bb_index)
Refactoring is identifier-aware static rewriting, not a full language-server proof

Per-mode argument rejection names the offending fields but not the accepted set for the mode (e.g. `bb_edit update mode does not accept: position` does not say that `update` accepts only `mode, dryRun, filePath, symbolName, lineStart, content/newContent, format`); callers must consult the mode contract in this page when constructing payloads. Known gap in `validateEditArguments` (src/mcp/tool-validation.ts). proof
tools.performance: Only affected files are written, formatted, validated, and reindexed.
tools.safety: Write-capable. Uses project-root path checks, atomic writes, snapshots, validation, and rollback; use dryRun before risky edits. dryRun writes no source file, but a stale target file is still refreshed in the INDEX first (derived data only), because the bounds it previews must be the bounds the real edit would use.
tools.evidence: Mutation bounds come from indexed AST bytes, re-resolved from the file on disk whenever the indexed rows are stale; validation and reindex state report whether post-edit evidence is current.

tools.name: bb_index
tools.description: Reindex a file or directory so the index reflects edits immediately (agent-fresh). Accepts a path (file or dir); a file reindexes only that file, a dir runs an incremental index of that dir (changed files only). mode=post re-runs the heavy derived-data phases (relationships/enrichment/gravity/taints/health) WITHOUT re-parsing — the remediation after edits on incremental paths. Returns indexed/deleted/error counts, or the per-phase post-processing report.

path.description: Project-relative file (reindex only that file) or directory (incremental index of changed files); for mode=post, the project whose derived phases should be re-run

mode.description: auto (default) infers file vs dir from path; file reindexes one file; dir runs an incremental directory index; post re-runs derived phases (relationships/taints/health) without re-parsing

documentation.summary: Immediately refresh the index for a just-written/edited file or directory; mode=post re-derives relationships/taints/health without re-parsing.

returns: Indexed, deleted, and error counts for the refreshed path
Mode actually applied (auto resolved, file, or dir)
Per-file error names for any file that failed to reindex
errors: Parse or store failure for an individual file
limitations: A file reindex updates only that file's evidence; cross-file relationships refresh on the next full or incremental dir index
Dir mode reuses the incremental indexer: unchanged files are skipped by design
tools.performance: A single file reindex is bounded by that file's parse cost; dir mode is bounded by the changed-file set.
tools.safety: Write-capable against index data only. It never modifies source files.
tools.evidence: Counts come from the real parse/store pipeline; errors name the file that failed rather than swallowing it.

tools.name: bb_graph
tools.description: Per-symbol dependency graph over the canonical graph engine: callers, callees, per-edge evidence tier (structural/import_based/usage_contextual/reference_qualified/inferred), confidence, and cross-language edge count. Same engine and tier rules the editor graph panel uses; truncated traversals are declared with a reason, never silent. Traversal semantics: a relationship stored against any member of a class (a method call, an inherited behavior) is attributed to the owner class, so caller/callee sets include the owner-family level — every edge still traces to a stored relationship row. Each edge's `rowId` is that stored key with its leading '<projectHash>:rel:' removed: the prefix is constant within one answer and is already readable as the segment before the first ':' of any `id` here, so prepending '<projectHash>:rel:' reconstructs the store key exactly. The stored key is 127-248 characters and was 28-31% of every edge's bytes.

symbol.description: symbol name to root the graph at (`target`/`symbolName`/`query` are accepted as aliases)

direction.description: which side to traverse (default both). 'callers' answers "who depends on this" and skips the callee walk entirely — on a real index that is the difference between 1 edge and 37 in the same payload.

relationshipTypes.description: stored relationship kinds to include. Default: EVERY kind the index stores (calls, extends, implements, uses, instantiates, overrides, contains, references, imports, exports) — deliberately not narrowed, because a narrower default silently drops a fifth of the graph and cannot descend a class hierarchy: 'contains' is the parent-to-member edge, so excluding it means a traversal rooted at a class cannot reach that class's own methods. The cost is size — the type-level 'uses'/'references'/'contains' rows are roughly half of what a typical index stores, so a hub symbol's default answer is 2.5-4.8x larger than a filtered one (measured: lodash 487 KiB against 101 KiB, ripgrep 795 against 321). Pass relationshipTypes: ['calls'] for the pure call graph, or ['implements'] to see only interface satisfaction; a kind you do not list is never reported, and a filter you supply is recorded in the answer's truncationReason so a filtered answer is never read as the whole graph.

includeCrossLanguage.description: include edges the indexer marked cross-language (default true). Set false for a single-language view.

timeBudgetMs.description: wall-clock budget for the whole walk in milliseconds (default 2000; 0 disables it). This is the one bound that is a function of the CLOCK rather than of the data, so a run that hits it can return fewer edges than an otherwise identical run moments later — `summary.timeBudgetExhausted` says when. Raise it, or set 0 to accept the runtime, when you need the whole set or a reproducible answer

maxEdges.description: hard cap on the number of edges in the WHOLE answer, across both directions and all depths (default 1000, max 5000). `edgeLimit` bounds one query and this bounds the answer; their product is what a caller receives. Reaching it is declared as `total-edge-limit` with the value in `summary.maxEdges`. Raise it for a hub symbol, lower it for a quick shape check

edgeLimit.description: Per-symbol call-site limit for one edge query (default 200, max 5000). Reaching it is declared in `summary.truncated` with `summary.truncationReason` and the root's true count in `summary.callersIfUncapped`/`summary.calleesIfUncapped` — the limit is never a silent cap. Raise it to receive more sites in one answer.

documentation.summary: Per-symbol graph with per-edge evidence tiers — the agent view of the editor's graph panel.

returns: Per-symbol dependency graph: callers and callees
Per-edge endpoints as described nodes — `{ id, name, symbolType, file, line, isExternal }` on BOTH ends, so an edge is self-contained and no id has to be parsed or looked up in a second call

Per-edge `rowId`: the stored `brain_relationship` row the edge came from, so every claim is auditable against the index (measured: every emitted rowId resolves to exactly one stored row, and the edge's endpoints agree with that row)
Endpoints the index could not resolve as `ext:<name>` nodes, with `isExternal: true` — a recorded name, never a symbol guessed from that name

Per-edge `match` (`exact` | `owner-cascade`) and `matchedMember` (`{ name, file }` when the cascade matched): whether the stored row names the symbol that was asked for, or one of its members folded onto it
Per-edge evidence tier (structural/import_based/usage_contextual/reference_qualified/inferred) with confidence

Per-edge call-site address (M62.A2): `{ kind, file, line, note }` — `call-site` is an exact stored line; `declaration` is a LABELED substitute (the calling symbol's own declaration, shown only when no call-site line is stored); `unknown` has no position at all (line null) and states why. A position is never fabricated and never reported as line 0

`summary.edgesByType`: the composition of the RETURNED edges by stored relationship kind, counted from the emitted edges. The default filter covers every stored kind, so an answer is usually not all call edges — measured: lodash `baseConvert` 99 of 230, cobra `getCompletions` 36 of 65, rake `standard_rake_options` 72 of 76. This is how you learn the ratio without walking the edges

`summary.maxEdges` / `totalEdgeLimitReached`: the bound on the WHOLE answer, across both directions and every depth, and whether it bit. `edgeLimit` bounds one query; this bounds the answer, and their product is what a caller receives

`summary.edgeKindPriority`: the order in which kinds survive the per-symbol site limit — dependency kinds first, then lexical, then module-level, then membership. Only observable under `truncated`, published always

`summary.relationshipTypesUsed`: the relationship kinds this run actually searched, resolved. `summary.scope.relationshipTypes` echoes it, so the filter that produced the answer is never a restatement of a default that may have moved

`summary.exactCallers` / `cascadedCallers` / `exactCallees` / `cascadedCallees`: DEPTH 0 only — how much of the answer is about the symbol that was asked for and how much the owner cascade folded in from its members. `deeperCallers` / `deeperCallees` hold the edges about symbols the traversal discovered, so exact + cascaded + deeper is the number of edges returned

`summary.callerBudget` / `calleeBudget` with `callerBudgetExhausted` / `calleeBudgetExhausted`: the fan-out bound in force and whether it bit. `truncationReason` can name `caller-budget-exhausted`; this says what the budget was
`summary.edgesInBothDirections`: stored rows present in both the caller and the callee list — `totalCallers + totalCallees` double-counts exactly this many
`root.candidates`: how many stored symbols the requested name resolved among — 1 means the name was unique, more means the answer is about one of several and `root` is what to confirm
`summary.maxDepth`: the depth bound this run actually used, alongside `summary.maxDepthReached`. Together they are the only way to tell "the walk finished" from "the walk stopped"
A per-edge `depth`, which is HOW FAR THE WALK WENT before finding that row — not the shortest distance between two symbols. See Limitations

`summary.scope`: the `direction`, `relationshipTypes` and `includeCrossLanguage` actually applied, so a narrowed traversal returning zero edges is distinguishable from a widened one that found nothing
Declared truncation with a reason when the traversal is bounded
errors: relationshipTypes given as an empty list (a narrowed traversal that can match nothing is refused rather than silently returning an empty graph)
Symbol not found in the index
limitations: Edges reflect indexed static evidence with declared tiers; inferred edges are labeled, not proven

An edge's `depth` is the depth of the query that found its stored row, not the shortest path between the two symbols. The traversal is depth-first and the per-row dedupe is global, so the first traversal to reach a row emits it: measured, 24% of edges on cobra, 57% on lodash and 60% on rake sit deeper than the shortest path in their own answer. No edge ever claims a SHORTER path than its answer can demonstrate, so `depth` is a valid upper bound on distance - read it as 'how far the walk got', not 'how far apart these are'. Use `direction` with a smaller `maxDepth` when the distance itself matters

The default filter covers every stored relationship kind, so an answer mixes dependency edges with lexical references (`uses`, `references`), structural membership (`contains`) and module edges (`imports`, `exports`). `contains` means owner → member: a class reporting its own methods is structure, not dependency. Filter with `relationshipTypes` for a pure call graph, or read `edgesByType`

Every kind competes for the per-symbol site limit, and the surviving set is decided by `edgeKindPriority` — dependency kinds first. A truncated answer therefore keeps more `calls` and fewer `contains` than an untruncated one would, and the published order is the rule that decides it

A target the index could not resolve appears as an `ext:<name>` node rather than as a symbol. That is a real gap in the index, surfaced rather than papered over: the edge `caller --calls--> ext:name` is what the store holds, and no internal symbol is substituted for it
The graph reflects the index as of the last index run

Owner-cascade attribution: a relationship stored against a class member (e.g. a call to a method) is reported toward the owner class, so caller/callee sets are a superset of exact-symbol-only matches. The superset is REDUCIBLE: every edge carries `match` (`exact` or `owner-cascade`) and, when cascaded, `matchedMember` naming the member the stored row actually referenced, and the summary carries the exact/cascade split. Measured on cobra, `Command` (182 methods) answers with 184 caller edges of which 24 name `Command` itself — a ratio no per-edge field alone makes obvious, and one no count in the payload revealed before the split existed. Every edge also carries the `rowId` it traces to

A target the index could not resolve is reported as an `ext:<name>` node — a NAME the index saw and could not attach to a symbol — and is never resolved by matching that name against other symbols in the project. The name is not unique there (measured on vscode, `match` names 37,876 stored symbols; on svelte, `end` names 437,570), so matching it would manufacture edges the store does not contain, crowd out the resolvable callees, and seed the traversal with a guess. `ext:` nodes are leaves: there is nothing stored about them to walk into

Two identical calls return identical answers unless the wall-clock bound fired in one of them, in which case `summary.timeBudgetExhausted` says so. Every other bound here — the per-query site limit, the fan-out budget, the total-answer bound, the depth — is a function of the data, so two identical calls on an unchanged index always agree

A symbol name is not a unique identifier. When one name matches several stored symbols the resolver takes the highest-gravity match (ties broken by lowest id, so the pick is reproducible rather than SQLite's whim) and says how many it chose between in `root.candidates` — measured: `build` in lodash resolves among 7, `code_block.go` in cobra among 50, `Command` among 1. When `root.candidates` is greater than 1 the graph is about ONE of those symbols, so confirm `root` is the one you meant before reading the edges. The other candidates are not listed

A name containing a SQL LIKE wildcard (`%`, `_`) is matched LITERALLY, not as a pattern: it either resolves to a symbol that genuinely contains those characters or is reported not found. It never widens into a match on an unrelated symbol

Call-site positions depend on the analyzer: an exact line is claimed only where the index stored a real line; a legacy 0 or a NULL line yields the declared `declaration` or `unknown` address instead (derived by src/intelligence/graph/line-address.ts — never an inline fallback)

`summary.totalCallers`/`totalCallees` are the RETURNED counts, not the totals. A per-symbol site limit (`edgeLimit`, default 200, max 5000) bounds one edge query; when it is reached the answer declares `truncated` with `truncationReason` naming the bound (`caller-site-limit` / `callee-site-limit`), `cappedQueries` says how many queries hit it, and `callersIfUncapped`/`calleesIfUncapped` carry the root's true site count (null when no cap was reached — never zero). Before M59.A12 (#888) the limit was silent: a symbol with 3,437 call sites answered 200 rows with `truncated: false`. The cap now fires only when rows were ACTUALLY dropped: the query asks for one row beyond the limit, so a symbol holding exactly `edgeLimit` sites is reported complete instead of falsely truncated
tools.performance: maxDepth (default 3, max 10) bounds traversal; per-edge evidence resolution is bounded by the returned subgraph. The answer is bounded at three levels and every level is declared: the per-query site limit (`edgeLimit`, default 200, max 5000), the fan-out budget (50 symbols per direction, `callerBudget`/`calleeBudget`) and the size of the WHOLE answer (`maxEdges`, default 1000, max 5000). The third exists because the product of the first two is not a number a reader can use: measured, ripgrep's `unwrap` returns 206 edges at depth 1, 454 at depth 3 and 702 at depth 5 - 228 KiB, 504 KiB and 770 KiB rendered. Reaching `maxEdges` is declared as `total-edge-limit` with the value in `summary.maxEdges`. A fourth bound is a wall-clock budget for the walk (`timeBudgetMs`, default 2000, 0 disables it), and it is the ONE bound here that is a function of the clock rather than of the data: a run that hits it can return fewer edges than an otherwise identical run moments later, and `summary.timeBudgetExhausted` says when. Measured, one run of cobra's busiest symbol at depth 3 rendered 526,043 bytes and the next 493,988. Raise `timeBudgetMs`, or set `0` to accept the runtime, when you need the whole set or a reproducible answer. The depth bound (`maxDepth`, paired with the `maxDepthReached` that says how far the walk actually got) is the fourth `direction` halves the work when only one side is wanted. `direction` halves the work when only one side is wanted — measured on cobra, a caller-only question about a symbol with 36 callees returned 1 edge instead of 37. The per-direction fan-out budget (50 symbols) is internal and is not exposed: truncation is declared in the summary when it bites.
tools.safety: Read-only. It does not modify source files or index data.
tools.evidence: Nodes and edges come from the canonical graph engine over brain_symbol and brain_relationship rows; each edge carries its evidence tier, its confidence, the `rowId` of the row it came from, and `match`/`matchedMember` saying whether the row names the traced symbol or one of its members. Every emitted rowId resolves to exactly one stored row and the edge's endpoints agree with that row — verified against an independent SQL oracle on real repositories. The declared totals are counted with the same query and the same noise filters as the returned edges, so a reported total is the number a caller would receive if no limit existed — verified against an independent SQL count on real repos (validation/m59/results/cap-real-corpus.json). Owner-cascade edges are auditable in the same way: `match` and `matchedMember` identify the member the stored row actually named, and the exact/cascade split in the summary is verified against an independent SQL count of direct-target rows on real repos (cobra: tool reports `exactCallers: 24`; oracle counts 24 direct caller rows for the same symbol).

tools.name: bb_impact
tools.description: Bounded reverse-dependency impact for one symbol via the same component the editor graph panel uses: declared node budget (200) and depth (5), truncation as a first-class field with reason, and a declared total that is the size of the set the answer is a prefix of — measured, not inferred, so an answer that is short of the whole set says so even when no bound fired. Unknown symbols are loud declared errors — an empty impact set is never invented. Owner-cascade applies: impact includes dependents attributed at class level, not only exact-symbol rows. The relationship kinds that count are named in every answer's `rule.relationshipTypes` and can be overridden; a dependent carries its evidence tier, cross-language flag, bridge and position.

symbol.description: symbol name to compute impact for (`target`/`symbolName`/`query` are accepted as aliases)

relationshipTypes.description: stored relationship kinds to count as dependencies. Default: calls, instantiates, extends, implements. A kind that is not listed is never reported, and the applied list is echoed in `rule.relationshipTypes` on every answer. This is the same control bb_graph has, so a caller who wants the type-level `uses`/`references` rows can ask for them on either door.

refresh.description: set false to skip the bounded staleness repair and answer from the existing index. When omitted, stale files inside the answer are repaired and the walk is re-run so the answer is not built from the rows the refresh replaced.

documentation.summary: Bounded impact with declared truncation — identical numbers to the editor's impact mode.

returns: The rule the answer was MEASURED under, in `rule`: which relationship kinds count as dependencies (the applied list is echoed here on every answer), the owner-cascade, the noise policy, and the depth

Whether the set is the WHOLE truth or a prefix of a larger one, and how that was established: the component measures the returned set against an unbounded walk of the same rule whenever truncation was declared or the walk reached the last expandable depth, and declares a prefix when they disagree — even when no bound fired. The same measurement reports each dependent at its SHORTEST path rather than at the depth the traversal's depth-first walk first reached it by, and `countVerification` says whether that measurement ran

Downstream dependents of the symbol with per-edge evidence tiers and confidence, cross-language flags, bridge mechanism, and each dependent's own position. Every one of those describes ONE stored row, and `evidenceAtDepth` says which path that row is on: `depth` is the MEASURED shortest path, while the engine that produced the set walks depth-first and stamps the first trace, so the two can name different rows (measured on nine repositories before this was fixed: 340 of 4 258 rows, 7.98%). The evidence is re-read at the reported depth, and where no row can be attributed every evidence field is null rather than quoted from a longer path

How the requested name became the root it walked: `rootMatch` carries the name asked for, whether the match was exact, a containment match, or the member→owner substitution, and how many stored symbols carry that exact name

The declared limits, from the component that owns them: `budget` (node budget, depth, and the THREE ceilings the declared total is computed under) and `traversal` (depth actually reached, the engine's own truncation state and reason, its per-query site limit, its capped-query count, and the root's uncapped caller count when computable). The two work ceilings (`totalScanCeiling`, `totalExpansionCeiling`) are properties of the INDEX, so the same question always gets the same answer; `totalTimeCeilingMs` is a property of the MACHINE, and it is the one bound that can make two identical calls differ — `countVerification.timedOut` says when that happened

`reproducible` — whether this answer would be the same if asked again. Every other bound this tool and the engine declare is a property of the INDEX (node budget, depth cap, per-query site limit, caller budget), so the same question on the same index gives the same answer. The exception is a TIME bound: the engine's 2 000 ms walk-time budget, and this tool's own 4 000 ms breaker on the counting walk. Measured on the lane's largest index, `bb_impact {symbol:"file"}` returned 142, 59, 142, 142, 59 rows over five identical calls, and the engine declares the cause on exactly the short ones. `reproducible: false` is published, and `truncationReason` then says so in words rather than leaving it to be inferred from a sibling clause

How completeness was established, in `countVerification`: `ran: false` means the walk never reached the depth boundary, so no node could have been blocked and every bound that could fire has declared itself — the set is the whole truth by construction, with no measurement paid for. `ran: true` means the set was measured against an unbounded walk of the same rule and the two agree. `timedOut: true` means the measurement stopped on the wall clock, which is the only published reason the same question can get two different answers

How each dependent is a dependent, per row, in `via`: `exact` (the stored row names the symbol asked about), `member` (it names one of its members — the owner cascade working as declared, with the member named in `viaMember`), or `range-folded` (it names neither, and the row is in the answer only because the cascade RANGE widened). `cascade` is the composition of the returned set by those three, or `null` when the index refused the member lookups it needs to establish it

`directCount` — the exact number of DIRECT dependents, or `null` when the counting walk hit a declared ceiling. `totalCountIfKnown` is the true transitive total under the same rule, or `null` for a declared unknown. Neither is ever smaller than `shownCount`. `rule.relationshipTypes` names the kinds that count, so a `uses` or `references` relationship that did not appear is explained rather than mysterious

Freshness: a per-dependent `stale` flag (`true`/`false`, or `null` when the file is not in the index at all) and a summary `freshness` envelope; `rootStale` declares the root's own file separately, since a stale root with fresh dependents is still a stale answer
Declared-absent result when the symbol is unknown — never an empty guess
errors: Symbol not found in the index
The named symbol exists but is not a traversable root (an enum member, a constant, a plain field) — a declared error naming the kind, never an empty set
relationshipTypes given as an empty list (a narrowed rule that can match nothing is refused rather than silently re-read as the default — the same refusal bb_graph raises)
limitations: Static impact analysis cannot establish runtime behavior

The answer is not always reproducible. The graph engine's caller traversal carries a 2 000 ms walk-time budget, so on a large index a time-bounded walk returns a smaller set than the same question would on an idle machine. This is the engine owner's declared trade-off, published on every answer as `reproducible: false` and named in `truncationReason`; a caller who needs a reproducible answer on a hub should narrow the question or raise the engine's `timeBudgetMs`. Measured: cargo `file` 59-142 rows, cargo `cargo` 172-178 rows, over identical repeated calls
Reflects the index as of the last index run; the freshness envelope states how far that is from the files on disk
Owner-cascade attribution applies: dependents through class-member relationships are attributed to the owner class

A truncated answer is a bounded PREFIX of the set, not a sample of it: the walk is depth-first, so a hub's 200 returned rows are an exploration order, not the 200 nearest dependents. `directCount` is the field that makes the shape readable. The set is then re-sorted by the SHORTEST path the measurement found, so `depth` is minimal rather than first-traced, but membership is still the walk's exploration order

The owner cascade is a RANGE over symbol ids, and a range widens: for a member `P:container:29` it covers [`P:container:`, `P:container;`) — the whole container — so every sibling of `29` is folded in with it. Measured, the range is a strict SUPERSET of the owner relation (it never loses a dependent the owner relation has) but it adds dependents the owner relation does not: ripgrep `RegexMatcher` answers 21 of which 7 are `range-folded` and 0 are real members, graphql-js `join` 9 of 128, lodash `call` 2 of 85. `cascade.rangeFolded` counts them, so the over-count is visible instead of silent. The walk that implements the range is the graph engine's and is not changed here
tools.performance: Two costs, bounded by different things, measured over 41 hub and mid-fan-in answers on eight real repositories (a machine that was NOT idle, so these are an upper bound): cold p50 298 ms / p95 1 777 ms / max 4 207 ms, warm p50 427 ms / p95 2 047 ms / max 3 488 ms; slowest cargo `all` 4 207/3 488 ms, cargo `file` 1 777/2 436 ms, svelte `flushSync` 1 508/2 047 ms. A COMPLETE answer pays for one engine walk and nothing else — the completeness verification is not paid for at all, because a node can only be lost at the depth boundary, so one query over the last level's nodes decides whether anything was and the unbounded walk runs only when that says maybe. A PREFIX answer additionally pays for the counting walk that makes the declared total honest: one statement per LEVEL rather than one per symbol, bounded by two WORK ceilings (50 000 scanned rows, 2 000 expansions) past which the total is a declared `null` rather than a number paid for with seconds, and by a 4 000 ms circuit breaker that no measured corpus reaches. The expansion ceiling is not what makes it fast or slow: eleven of twelve hubs give an exact total at 300 expansions at the same wall time as at 2 000, and the ones that stay unknown do so at every ceiling because their closures are wide rather than deep.
tools.safety: Read-only. It does not modify source files or index data.
tools.evidence: Impact derives from brain_relationship rows via the same engine the editor impact panel uses. The declared total is measured by an independent bounded walk under the traversal's own rule — same relationship kinds, same owner cascade, same noise policy, same depth — so it is the size of the set the answer is a prefix of. Completeness is PROVED rather than inferred: whenever truncation was declared, or the walk reached the last expandable depth, the set is measured against an unbounded walk and declared a prefix when the two disagree, which is how cobra `HasAvailableFlags` came to answer 28 with `truncated: true` instead of 27 with `truncated: false`. An independent SQL oracle in the bb_impact corpus lane re-derives both the set and the total from the stored tables on nine real repositories, with an SQL-level differential between the cascade range rule and the owner relation behind the `via` numbers above.

tools.name: bb_cross_language
tools.description: Cross-language facts for one symbol from stored brain_relationship rows only (is_cross_language = 1), per-pair with bridge mechanism and evidence tier. Every fact names both ends — the copy of the requested name it came from and the other symbol's name, file, language and line — plus the stored row id. A name is many symbols (the index holds one per file/name/line), so facts are the union over every copy; `copies` names them and `ambiguous` says so. SEPARATELY, `memberFacts` holds the rows on the copies' MEMBERS, each marked `match: 'owner-cascade'` with `matchedMember` naming the member: 95% of stored cross-language rows target a member, so a class often has none of its own, and those rows are reported as the MEMBER's edges rather than absorbed into the symbol's — `ownFactCount`, `memberFactCount` and `silentItselfButNotItsMembers` tell the two apart. Absence is declared only when neither the copies nor their members hold a stored row. The answer is bounded by `limit` (default 200, max 1000) with `truncated` and `totalCountIfKnown` declared. This tool never infers, guesses, or aspires. Same source and laws as the editor's cross-language hover section.

symbol.description: symbol name to fetch cross-language facts for (`target`/`symbolName`/`query` are accepted as aliases)

limit.description: max facts to return (default 200, max 1000); truncation is declared, never silent

documentation.summary: Stored cross-language pairs, each naming both ends, with member rows reported separately, and declared absence and truncation.

returns: One fact per stored cross-language row about the name. `facts` holds the rows on the copies themselves; `memberFacts` holds the rows on their MEMBERS, each marked `match: "owner-cascade"` with `matchedMember` and `matchedMemberId` naming the member. Every fact names both ends — `self` (symbol, file, language, line) and `other` — plus the stored `rowId`, direction, bridge, evidence tier and confidence
`copies`: every indexed symbol carrying the name, with file, language, line and cross-row count, plus `ambiguous` and `ambiguityNote`

`ownFactCount` and `memberFactCount` separately, so a reader can tell a symbol that is itself connected from one that is connected only through its members — and `silentItselfButNotItsMembers` when that is the case

Declared absence only when NEITHER the copies nor their members hold a stored row, with `absenceNote` saying so — and saying so SCOPED TO THE PROJECT, because that is all the three queries behind it searched. It reads "anywhere in THIS PROJECT's index", because it used to read "anywhere in the index" while searching one project, which was false whenever the same name existed in another project holding rows for it (M63.CL4)

Declared truncation: `truncated`, `truncationReason` and `totalCountIfKnown` when the `limit` bounded the answer. `unpairableRowCount` and `collapsedRowCount` are GUARDS, not activity: each is 0 on all 1,662 names across two measured corpora, because the store as written cannot produce either state (see the limitations). They are verified by seeding the state each one guards, and both can be broken, so they are known to work rather than assumed to
errors: Symbol not found in the index (declared, not an empty set)
limit outside the declared 1..1000 range (refused, never clamped silently)
limitations: Reads stored is_cross_language=1 relationship rows only; never infers cross-language facts. Absence means "no stored rows FOR THIS PROJECT", never "this symbol is unconnected": the same name in another project may hold rows for it, which is why the absence note names the scope
Reads stored is_cross_language=1 relationship rows only; never infers cross-language facts
Coverage depends on the analyzers that produced cross-language rows — this tool reports what was stored, nothing more
A name is many symbols: the answer is the UNION over every copy, never a silent choice among them. Narrow with the `copies` list — every fact names the copy it came from

`collapsedRowCount` is 0 everywhere and is expected to be. It needs a row matched by BOTH the by-name query and the owner-cascade query, which needs a member named exactly like its owner — and the member query excludes that case by its own `m.name <> owner.name` filter, so the SQL forbids it rather than the data being empty. It is verified by seeding two same-named symbols in files of different languages, which does satisfy both arms; a self-edge does not, because one file means one language and the row is dropped as unpairable first. A mutant that removes the rule is caught

MEMBER ROWS ARE REPORTED, NOT ABSORBED. 95.4% of stored cross-language rows target a member rather than a class or namespace, so a by-name answer for an owner finds almost nothing on the owner itself. Those rows appear in `memberFacts`, attributed to the member, because an edge on `Label.newLabel` is not an edge on `Label`. bb_graph answers the same question by CASCADING member edges onto the owner, so its count is larger: its cascade is a lexical id-prefix range, this tool's is the store's `owner_symbol_id`. Both are declared; neither is reconciled into the other

`bridge` is the stored `bridge_mechanism`. On a real polyglot corpus it is almost always the indexer's `name-resolution` placeholder, which means two identifiers matched by name — not that the two languages communicate by that mechanism. Weigh it with `tier` and `confidence`

A row whose endpoint file has no detected language cannot name a pair; such rows are counted in `unpairableRowCount` and never dressed up with a guessed language. No corpus reaches that state — all 922 indexed files carry a language, and the indexer flags a row cross-language only when the two files' languages differ — so the guard is verified by seeding an unlabelled endpoint, and a mutant that fabricates a pair for it is caught
Over half of the stored cross-language rows on the measured corpus carry no analyzer evidenceClass, so their tier is derived by the shared rule rather than claimed by the analyzer
tools.performance: Three indexed queries — the stored rows for the name, the rows on its members, and every symbol carrying the name — with no graph traversal; every declared count is derived from the rows those three already returned, so there is no fourth query for it. Measured on a 230-file JVM corpus: the mean answer is 7 facts and 7.5KB, p90 is 12 facts, and the response is bounded by `limit`. For scale, `bb_graph` returns 3-8x more bytes for the same symbols, and on owner-heavy symbols it took 29-79s where this tool takes 14-53ms.
tools.safety: Read-only. It does not modify source files or index data.
tools.evidence: Only brain_relationship rows with is_cross_language=1, filtered by the ROW's own project_id — in both this tool and the editor cross-language hover section, which previously joined the opposite symbol with `ss.project_id = r.project_id` and so returned another project's rows; both directions of that fix are proved load-bearing by mutants that each remove one of them. Classified by the single evidence-tier rule in src/lsp/evidence_tier.ts, over a projection that names both ends because a hover card already shows which file the reader is in and an agent does not. Every count is cross-checked against an independent SQL count over two real polyglot indexes — a 230-file JVM corpus (3 language pairs) and a 692-file Elixir/Erlang corpus (16 pairs, 1,168 cross-language rows) — and thirteen planted defects are all caught on both, including three specific to the member section (cascade laundered, the pre-CL2 absence rule, and a cascade reported with no member to check it against) and two that break one direction of the hover door's project scope. Four further surfaces are covered that no corpus reaches — a project with no cross-language rows at all, a truncation driven by the member section, the own-first precedence rule at limit 1, and the absence note's project scope, the last of which found a real defect — bringing the total to fourteen planted defects: script/m63/verify-cl1-cross-language.ts, validation/m63/results/CL1.json. A corpus-free check that every mutant still has a live anchor runs in `verify:fast` as script/m63/verify-cl1-wiring.ts.

tools.name: bb_annotate
tools.description: Attach an agent-authored annotation to a symbol in the shared index. Provenance is enforced: the row records author class 'agent' (never spoofable), the calling tool identity, and timestamps. Re-annotating the same symbol+path updates the note in place — one note per author per location, enforced by a unique index over (project, symbol, author, path). The symbol is NOT checked against the index, so a note may name anything; instead the reply MEASURES whether an editor surface can show it and says so in `surfacing` (`editor`, `matchedAs`, `matchedNames`, `statement`) — a typo'd name or a qualified name is stored and reported honestly rather than promised to a surface it cannot reach. `path` is resolved to the index's own spelling, so `src/a.ts`, `./src/a.ts` and the absolute path are the same note. Annotations are opinions layered on evidence, never index facts. To change source code use bb_edit; to read notes back use bb_annotations.

symbol.description: symbol name to annotate (`target`/`query` are accepted as aliases)

path.description: optional file path to disambiguate same-named symbols; resolved to the index's own spelling (`brain_file.relative_path`), so `src/a.ts`, `./src/a.ts` and the absolute path all reach the same note

toolIdentity.description: optional name of the calling agent/tool (recorded verbatim)

documentation.summary: Agent note with enforced provenance, stored where the human reads.

examples.body: Legacy auth path — scheduled for removal in Q3.

returns: Stored annotation row with its enforced provenance (author class `agent`, never spoofable) and the calling tool identity, recorded verbatim

`surfacing` — whether an editor surface can actually show this note, MEASURED against the index rather than promised: `editor` (bool, the AND of `nameMatched` and `pathMatched` — the editor needs BOTH), `nameMatched`, `pathMatched`, `matchedAs` (`name` and/or `qualifiedName`), `matchedNames`, and a `statement` saying what is and is not true. The name matching is necessary but not sufficient: a note on a symbol the index holds, written against a path it has never seen, can never be selected by a file-scoped hover, and is reported `editor: false` with the reason. This replaced a `surfaces` field that claimed the note "renders in the editor hover section and graph badge" for every note; measured on a real corpus, 100% of notes written under a symbol's qualified name matched no symbol name at all, so that claim was false exactly where it sounded most confident

The path handling: `surfacing.pathNote` when a path was resolved to the index's own spelling, `surfacing.pathWarning` when no indexed file matches the given path (stored under that spelling, no editor surface will scope it to a file), and a name-level note statement when no path was given
errors: Empty body (a refusal, not a silent no-op)
Body exceeds the declared 2000-char limit, counted in characters (an astral glyph is one character, not two UTF-16 units)
toolIdentity exceeds the declared 200-char limit — refused, never truncated

toolIdentity containing a control character or line break — a label is a name, not a document. Refused, because a newline in that field rendered (measured, through the real renderer) as a SECOND provenance line that could claim to be a human note
limitations: Annotations are opinions layered on index evidence, never index truth
Annotation store semantics are owned by the M28 workstream
Any symbol name is accepted. Reachability is reported, not enforced: a name no indexed symbol carries is stored and declared `surfacing.editor: false`

The note is keyed on the name as given. A name that matches several indexed symbols (a name is one symbol per file/line — `force` in 8 files of a real corpus) is one note shown wherever that name appears, unless `path` scopes it to a file
